title: The Whale Behind $29.75 Million in Wins Just Went Long on Ethereum
summary: A Hyperliquid whale with $29.75 million in profits opened a $60.7 million Ethereum long as price weakens and ETF outflows hit 10 days.
content:
Leveraged bulls lost $688.56 million to liquidations in a single day as Ethereum (ETH) and Bitcoin (BTC) slid. One Hyperliquid whale with a near-flawless record has stepped into that selloff with a big long bet.

The trader has opened ETH longs worth about $60.7 million. Those positions already sit on roughly $2.6 million in unrealized profit, Lookonchain data showed.

The whale built that record quickly. It created 4 new wallets about 4 months ago and began trading on Hyperliquid, a decentralized derivatives exchange.

Since then, the trader has closed 15 trades with only 1 loss, according to data shared by Lookonchain. That loss was $3,866 on an ETH short held for 1 minute.

Most of the whale's profit came from BTC longs, which brought in about $28.2 million of the $29.75 million total.

"Meet this mysterious whale who has won almost all 15 trades, making a total profit of $29.75M!" Lookonchain posted.

However, 2 of the whale's older positions are still losing money. A 10,000 ETH long shows a $1.9 million loss, while a 400 BTC long is down about $97,000.

After netting those losses against the new longs, all 4 open positions sit about $608,600 in profit.

Follow us on X to get the latest news as it happens

The whale is betting on an asset that has swung sharply over the past week. ETH traded at $2,526.75 at press time, BeInCrypto Markets data showed.

That price leaves ETH down 0.99% over 24 hours and 6.39% over 7 days.

ETH dipped near $2,429 earlier on Tuesday as liquidations swept the market. The whale's new entries, near $2,420, sit close to that level.

Meanwhile, US spot Ethereum exchange-traded funds (ETFs) have moved the other way. They have recorded 10 straight days of net outflows, according to SoSoValue data.

Withdrawals since September 29 total about $782.6 million. The streak began right after roughly $437 million in inflows during the week of September 22.

On the charts, analyst Ted Pillows flagged the level ETH needs to clear for a bigger move.

If ETH stalls below the $2,560 to $2,570 zone, the whale still has room. Its liquidation prices sit near $1,272 and $1,513, far below current levels.

The next test comes from US inflation data. The September Consumer Price Index (CPI) report lands on Wednesday.

Economists expect annual inflation to rise to 3.7% from 3.4%. A hotter print could pressure leveraged longs, while a softer one could support ETH's rebound.

title: Cleveland Fed President Wants Small, Quick Rate Moves. What It Means for Bitcoin
summary: Fed’s Hammack backs restrictive policy as December hike odds near 85% and Bitcoin slips in its strongest quarter.
content:
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said that restrictive monetary policy is appropriate to return inflation to 2%. She also favors making smaller rate adjustments quickly rather than waiting and risking a larger correction later.

Rate futures now point to a hike in December, and the US dollar sits near an 18-month high. Meanwhile, Bitcoin (BTC) has slipped in October, historically one of its strongest months.

Hammack, a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), spoke at the National Association for Business Economics annual meeting. She said the breadth of current price pressures means inflation will take some time to reach 2%.

August data shows the size of that gap. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.4% annually. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, came in at 3%.

Inflation has now run above target for more than five years. Hammack said long-run inflation expectations have stayed anchored through that stretch, but she warned against taking that for granted.

"With each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risks of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy," Hammack said.

The Fed has already started tightening. It raised rates in September for the first time in 3 years, and minutes from that meeting signaled another hike without a timeline. Hammack also raised the prospect of hikes in July, linking artificial intelligence (AI) demand to price pressure.

Follow us on X to get the latest news as it happens

Traders expect that next hike to come in December. CME FedWatch data shows an 84.7% chance of a move at the December 9 meeting.

Most of that probability, 69%, sits on a 25 basis point hike. For October 28, traders see a 79.5% chance of a hold, up from 51% a month earlier.

Those hike bets have lifted the US Dollar Index (DXY) to an 18-month high. Higher rates make dollar assets more attractive, which can draw money away from riskier markets such as crypto.

Bitcoin trades at $81,661, down 2.56% over the past 24 hours, according to BeInCrypto Markets. That leaves BTC about 35% below its all-time high of $126,080, set on October 6, 2025.

CoinGlass data shows BTC is down 1.89% so far in October. The month has historically been one of Bitcoin's strongest, with only 3 red Octobers since 2013: 2014, 2018 and 2025.

October also opens Q4, which has averaged a 71.43% gain since 2013, the highest of any quarter. Wednesday's September Consumer Price Index (CPI) data gives traders a fresh read before the Fed meets on October 28.

Futures also assign a 15.7% chance to a larger 50 basis point hike in December. Whether that tail grows or fades could decide if Bitcoin salvages its October.

title: Bulls Absorb 89% of $774 Million Crypto Liquidations as Leverage Unwinds
summary: Crypto liquidations hit $774 million, with longs taking 89% as Bitcoin slid below $82,000 ahead of US CPI data.
content:
Leveraged bulls took the brunt of a $774.14 million crypto liquidation wave over the past 24 hours, losing $688.56 million.

Those traders were caught on the wrong side of the selloff, as macro and geopolitical factors weighed on markets, and a sharp stock rout in Asia added to the strain.

BeInCrypto Markets data showed the total crypto market cap fell 4.40% to $2.77 trillion over the past 24 hours. Bitcoin (BTC) dropped 2.67% to $81,594, while Ethereum (ETH) lost 4.46% to $2,429.16.

Altcoins fell further, with Solana (SOL) declining 7.11% to $103.62 and Zcash (ZEC) sliding 9.54%.

The drop caught traders betting on higher prices. CoinGlass data showed 172,662 traders liquidated, with longs making up 88.9% of the total and shorts accounting for $85.58 million.

Ethereum led with $169.23 million in liquidations, 86.3% of them longs. Bitcoin followed at $160.48 million, with longs at 90.2%. Solana saw $60.41 million wiped out, 94.2% of it longs.

The largest single order was a $9.65 million BTCUSDT long on Binance, liquidated at $81,772.75. Binance handled 51.9% of all liquidations.

While longs took heavy losses, some traders who bet on a decline sat on notable gains. Blockchain analytics account Lookonchain flagged AguilaTrades, a trader with $38 million in total losses, opening a 40x short on 124.24 BTC.

The decline came as the Middle East conflict escalated. Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have killed at least 20 people in a week, including a US national, CBS reported.

President Donald Trump has said the US may join Saudi Arabia's offensive against the Houthis in Yemen.

Inflation worries also hung over markets. Treasury yields sit near 24-year highs, raising the appeal of bonds over non-yielding assets.

Meanwhile, Asian equities came under heavy pressure. South Korea's KOSPI fell nearly 5% on Tuesday as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix slid.

Tom Lee, who chairs Ethereum treasury firm BitMine, linked the Korean slump to crypto's losses.

The next test comes Wednesday, when the US releases its September Consumer Price Index (CPI) report. Economists expect annual inflation to rise to 3.7% from 3.4%.

A hotter print could strengthen rate-hike bets and add selling pressure, while softer inflation could ease them.

With longs carrying nearly 89% of the losses, Wednesday's data may decide whether leveraged bulls rebuild or retreat further.

title: When Will Bitcoin Price Reclaim Its All-Time High? Cycle Data Gives a Date
summary: Cycle data shows how fast Bitcoin could reclaim its ATH. See why mid-2027 is the deadline and 2028 the likely peak.
content:
Bitcoin price currently trades 35% below its record peak of $126,000. When will BTC again reclaim its all-time high?

Based on market cycle patterns, popular analyst Root suggests it could be by June 2027. Here's how the analyst comes up with this timeline.

Root, who writes the Bitcoin Strategy newsletter, compared the current recovery with three previous cycles.

Historically, Bitcoin needed around 2 years from the bottom to enter a phase of setting new highs.

However, the last cycle broke that pattern. The spot ETF approval pushed BTC to fresh highs far earlier.

"If Bitcoin follows a similar recovery trajectory as previous cycles, instead of the historical two years, we should reach new ATHs by around the one-year mark at the latest, around June 2027."

His chart shows the 2015, 2018, and 2022 cycles all moved above the scaled ATH level by roughly day 350.

The 2018 cycle got there first, near day 150. Therefore, Root sees a possible window roughly two to six months from now.

The current setup also asks less of the market. Bitcoin fell roughly 52% from its October 2025 peak to a 2026 low near $60,000.

In contrast, the previous three bear markets erased between 77% and 85% of BTC's value. As a result, Bitcoin needs only about a 2x move from its bottom to set a new record.

Past cycles completed a comparable move within about a year. This timing also fits other halving cycle signals.

Analyst Philarekt offers a longer view. On the three-week chart, BTC has traded inside one ascending channel since 2021.

According to the analyst, every bottom and every top has formed higher than the last. The 2026 low bounced off channel support, and the next ATH on the chart sits near $170,000.

Notably, his projected path also shows BTC briefly clearing $126,000 around mid-2027. The full cycle peak then arrives in 2028, which broadly aligns with Root's timeline.

Both models depend on the bottom being in. Binance Research found that similar rebounds retested their lows in four of five past cases.

Returns are also shrinking. The 2021 to 2025 move between peaks was about 83%, while a $170,000 top would deliver roughly 35%. Moreover, each channel boundary rests on only two touches.

Some analysts question the cycle itself. Willy Woo has argued Bitcoin may abandon the four-year rhythm for a longer TradFi cycle. Root also flags rising rates and their effect on the business cycle.

Taken together, the data suggest BTC could reclaim $126,000 in 2027, while the larger cycle peak may wait until 2028.

title: A year after crypto’s $19 billion crash, one warning sign still hasn’t gone away
summary: Bitcoin is still more than 30% below its record, and market insiders say the problem that made last October’s crash so brutal is still there.
content:
One year after crypto's worst single-day wipeout, the market has cooled. But the risk that made it so painful has not fully disappeared.

On Oct. 10, 2025, more than $19 billion in leveraged bets were liquidated in a single day. Bitcoin has since struggled to recover and remains more than 30% below its all-time high.

For Julia Zhou, president of crypto market maker Caladan, the bigger problem last October was not the size of the losses. It was how fast buyers and sellers vanished when the market needed them most .

Traders are now more aware of the risks, she told Bloomberg. But she warned that the market is still "highly fragmented" and that liquidity "can still deteriorate rapidly."

Related: If you invested $1,000 in Bitcoin when Trump took office in 2017 vs 2025, here's how much you'd have made or lost

Traders have been slow to return to borrowed bets. Open interest in Bitcoin perpetual futures, a measure of leveraged trading, stood near $45 billion a year ago. It more than halved within six months of the crash, according to CryptoQuant data cited by Bloomberg.

Analysts don't see a quick breakout either. QCP Capital expects Bitcoin to trade between $80,000 and $90,000 for the rest of the year.

Some analysts are also watching the US midterm elections. Crypto analyst Ali Charts noted last month that Bitcoin fell between 27% and 72% after each of the past four midterms.

He flagged $73,000 as a key level to watch, though he said the elections did not necessarily cause those drops.

In 2011, Bitcoin fell 94% from $32 to near zero after the Mt. Gox hack. The obituaries were written . It recovered to hit $1,163.

From late 2013 to early 2015, Bitcoin fell about 85% , from $1,133 to roughly $170. It was the longest crash in Bitcoin's history, and the price didn't set a new record until March 2017, more than three years later.

When the ICO bubble burst, Bitcoin fell from a peak near $20,000 in December 2017 to $3,122 a year later , a drop of about 84%. Every retail investor who bought near the top was underwater for years. The market recovered anyway.

March 2020 was brutal and brief. Bitcoin lost nearly half its value in a single day during the COVID panic, falling below $4,000 . By December it had passed $20,000 , beating its 2017 record.

In May 2021, $1 trillion was wiped from crypto in a single week. Bitcoin had touched $64,000 in April.

Then came 2022, the worst in recent memory. Bitcoin had peaked near $69,000 in November 2021. It fell to about $17,600 after Terra Luna imploded, then to about $15,500 as FTX went under.Signs the market has changed

Not everyone is gloomy. Leverage is lower than a year ago, and some exchanges have strengthened their systems for handling forced selling.

VanEck's Matthew Sigel has also noted that Bitcoin's volatility has dropped by about half compared with four years ago.

As per Bloomberg, Galaxy Digital's Lucas Tcheyan went further, saying the market that crashed on Oct. 10 "doesn't really exist anymore."

title: FTX’s old Bitcoin mining assets have a new mission, and it’s not crypto
summary: A Bitcoin miner once tangled in the FTX collapse is being rebuilt as an AI data-center business.
content:
The Bitcoin-mining business once stuck in the FTX's bankruptcy getting a second life, powering AI, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.

SWI Group, which took over the former Genesis Digital Assets this summer, announced Monday it has raised 800 million euros, which is about $900 million.

The Amsterdam-listed, Singapore-incorporated company had a market value of around $6 billion as of Oct 9. CEO Max-Hervé George said SWI needs capital to deploy more compute and has "zero interest" in Bitcoin mining.

The firm wants to serve hyperscalers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud from sites in Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina and Sweden. It is also selling its last Kazakhstan assets, three small mining sites, reports the WSJ.

Related: Dave Ramsey's investing advice falls short, study finds

Founded in 2017, Genesis Digital grew into one of the world's largest Bitcoin miners. Sam Bankman-Fried's Alameda Research invested more than $1 billion from 2021 and held a 20% stake. After FTX filed for bankruptcy in November 2022, the company faced weak Bitcoin prices and a hostile Kazakh government.

FTX's administrators sued last year to claw back $1.15 billion. They dropped the case on June 15, the same day SWI said it had spent $500 million on a major stake .

As reported by the Wall Street Journal, the SWI has since become majority owner, and George said all related legal disputes are settled.

Bankman-Fried is serving a 25-year sentence for fraud, yet some of his investments look better now.

His $500 million Anthropic bet in 2021 gave FTX a 7.8% stake, which the estate sold for $1.3 billion in 2024. At the AI company's latest valuation , it would be worth about $75 billion.

title: US Dollar Hits 18-Month High: What It Means for Bitcoin and Stocks
summary: The dollar hit an 18-month high as traders bet on a December Fed hike. See what Wednesday's CPI could change.
content:
The US dollar is surging, and that could spell trouble for Bitcoin and Wall Street. The US Dollar Index (DXY) reached an 18-month high near 102.56 on Monday, while Bitcoin struggled around $83,000 and the Nasdaq slipped.

Behind the dollar's rally is a growing expectation that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again this year. Higher rates make dollar-based investments more attractive, potentially pulling money away from riskier markets.

Bitcoin pays no interest. When US government bonds offer yields above 5%, investors have more reason to move money into safer assets.

A stronger dollar can also reduce demand for speculative investments, particularly cryptocurrencies and high-growth technology stocks.

The pressure is already visible. Bitcoin lost nearly 3% over the past week, while Ethereum suffered larger losses. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq slipped on Monday, with higher oil prices adding pressure.

The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.35% on October 8, its highest in 24 years. Investors also moved $166 billion into money-market funds that week.

The Fed's benchmark rate currently stands at 3.75%–4%. Futures pricing indicates roughly an 87% chance of another hike by December, although most traders expect no change in October.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack warned that persistent inflation could become increasingly difficult to control.

"With each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risks of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy," Hammack stated.

Wednesday's CPI report could determine the next market move. Economists expect annual inflation to reach 3.7%, up from 3.4%, while core prices are forecast to rise 0.2% monthly.

Higher-than-expected inflation could strengthen the dollar further, adding selling pressure to Bitcoin and stocks. Softer inflation could offer some relief by reducing expectations of additional rate hikes.

Even Goldman Sachs, which upgraded global equities on Monday, identified higher interest rates as a key near-term risk.

title: Can Cardano Reach $1 Before Bitcoin Reaches $100,000?
summary: Cardano needs a fourfold surge while Bitcoin chases a relatively modest gain, but the race to these milestone prices is far less straightforward than the numbers suggest. One coin carries a hidden weight that could derail its climb before it even gets started.

title: Litecoin Has Beaten Bitcoin for 30 Days Straight. The Last Three Times It Did, the Lead Ended the Same Way.
summary: Litecoin has outpaced Bitcoin before, and each time the story ended the same way. With a new fund and a halving on the horizon, bulls are convinced this time is different, but the past week already raised a red flag.

Litecoin outpaced Bitcoin by 13 points over 30 days, but its three prior leads from 2017, 2021, and 2023 all ultimately faded.

Litecoin's 7% weekly drop versus Bitcoin's 3% signals speculative rotation, matching its historical pattern of rising fast and falling hard.

However, in the past week, both cryptocurrencies took a hit, complicating the picture. Litecoin fell 7%, while Bitcoin fell 3.2%. As a result, Litecoin currently trades around $65, about 84% below its peak of $410.

Historically, Litecoin has outperformed Bitcoin before, but its lead has consistently faded over time. The key question is whether Litecoin can maintain its current advantage over Bitcoin this time.

Litecoin is a payments-focused cryptocurrency, originally a faster, lighter branch of Bitcoin's code. Because its market capitalization is significantly smaller than Bitcoin's, even a modest influx of new investment can drive its price much higher.

Traders looking for larger gains often shift their money from Bitcoin into altcoins — any cryptocurrency that isn't Bitcoin. This shift is known as rotation. Three previous instances followed a similar pattern: Litecoin surged in December 2017, again in spring 2021, and rallied ahead of its 2023 halving. However, each time, Litecoin eventually surrendered its lead over Bitcoin. While these patterns suggest a tendency, they are based on just a few instances over nearly a decade.

This time around, Litecoin has two significant developments: a halving expected in 2027, which will reduce the rewards for miners, thereby decreasing the new supply of coins entering the market; and a new Litecoin fund from a major asset manager that allows investors to gain exposure to Litecoin without needing to hold the actual coin.

Litecoin's current advantage over Bitcoin will likely diminish, as it did after the spikes in December 2017, spring 2021, and 2023. Although the fund and upcoming halving are promising developments, they still haven't given Litecoin enough stability to withstand drops as well as Bitcoin. Typically, during market rotations, smaller coins rise quickly but fall sharply when confidence wanes, and the past week reflects that pattern.

For Litecoin holders, two key changes need to happen for its lead to seem sustainable. First, Litecoin must stop decreasing faster than Bitcoin during downturns. content:
Zcash dipped on Monday, while Cypherpunk Technologies' CIO Will McEvoy said ZEC mining earned roughly four times what AI hosting paid.

He said supply was tight because Bitmain was the only company that made Zcash mining machines, and new orders could take seven to eight months or longer to arrive.

Zcash (ZEC) edged lower on Monday, while an executive at Winklevoss-backed Cypherpunk Technologies (CYPH) said mining the privacy token was far more profitable than mining Bitcoin (BTC) or hosting AI.

Zcash mining earned about $1,000 per megawatt hour, Cypherpunk Chief Investment Officer (CIO) Will McEvoy said on the Bankless podcast. On the other hand, Bitcoin miners have been shifting power to AI customers, pushing investors to reprice them .

That shift lifted many Bitcoin miners from about $130 per megawatt hour to around $240, McEvoy said. He called it "a good step up," but said Zcash mining paid roughly four times as much. Profit per megawatt hour showed how much a miner earned from each unit of electricity, which let it compare one business against another.

ZEC's price was down over 1% during the past 24 hours, after giving back its earlier gains of 4% . On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around ZEC remained in the 'extremely bearish' zone, while chatter stayed at 'low 'levels over the past day.

McEvoy said Cypherpunk shouldn't be valued like a typical crypto treasury company. With the warrants included, the company had an enterprise value of about $1 billion, roughly split between its $500 million in ZEC and its mining business, he said.

McEvoy said the profit stayed high because only a few machines could mine Zcash. Bitmain was the only company that made them, and it likely produced only a few thousand a month. He said a new order would take around 7 to 8 months to arrive, and "probably longer than that."

McEvoy added that Bitmain had little reason to make more. Zcash was a small business for the company next to its Bitcoin machines. Any newcomer would have to design its own chips and compete with AI companies for factory space at chip makers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (TSMC).

Cypherpunk controls about 18% of Zcash computing power, or hash rate, and calls its fleet the largest Zcash mining operation in the world. McEvoy said the company planned to keep that share at 18% to 20%.

The company held around 323 thousand ZEC as of August, standing at roughly 1.92% of the 21 million token supply, according to a filing.

Cypherpunk aims to own 5% of the ZEC supply, similar to the target that has driven Tom Lee's Bitmine Immersion (BMNR) with Ethereum (ETH), popularly known as the " Alchemy of 5% ."

title: Solana Treasury Firm DeFi Development Keeps Buying SOL as CHAD Preferred Stock Hits Record
summary: The Nasdaq-listed company now holds about 2.59 million SOL, but its weekly purchases keep shrinking.
content:
DeFi Development Corp, the Nasdaq-listed Solana piggy bank, added about 22,070 SOL—worth about $2,373,211—and "SOL equivalents" to its treasury last week, according to a press release published Monday.

That brings its stash to roughly 2,586,282 tokens, worth about $287 million with SOL near $111. Weekly buys keep shrinking , from 101,381 SOL in mid-September (around $11.4 million) to 47,706 ($5.8 million), then 26,202 ($3.1 million).

DFDV is a digital asset treasury company, a public firm that holds a cryptocurrency so stock investors can bet on it without opening a crypto account. It was a real estate software firm called Janover until April 2025, when it pivoted to Solana and copied Strategy's Bitcoin playbook.

CHAD, the company's perpetual preferred stock, hit all-time highs in the week ended October 9 and is approaching $10. Perpetual preferred shares never mature and get dividends before common stock; CHAD pays a variable 13% a year on its $10 stated amount, or $1.30 per share, declared each business day.

"CHAD reaching new highs and approaching $10.00 even as SOL pulled back is an encouraging sign that investors are recognizing its distinct income proposition," said Dan Kang, Chief Strategy Officer. "For common shareholders, CHAD provides a funding source that can support accretive SOL per share growth without issuing additional common shares. For CHAD holders, it offers daily income supported by that growing, productive treasury," he added.

That record sounds less dramatic once you know the shares priced their IPO at $8 in September, below their own stated amount. Last week DFDV even authorized buybacks for whenever CHAD trades under its $10 par value. Mission nearly accomplished.

The price matters because DFDV funds its SOL purchases through a $300 million at-the-market program, which sells new CHAD shares gradually at market prices. The closer CHAD trades to $10, the more SOL each new share buys.

"Short-term volatility has not changed our conviction or our commitment to accumulating SOL," CEO Joseph Onorati said in the release.

SOL fell about 9% over seven days, and nearly $1 billion in long positions, or bets that prices would rise, were liquidated in 24 hours. Liquidation is forced selling: when traders bet with borrowed money and prices fall far enough to wipe out their collateral, exchanges close the bet automatically, pushing prices lower still.

A 13% dividend looks generous, but CHAD is backed by a company whose main asset trades about 62% below its January 2025 peak of roughly $295. The release itself warns that staking rewards may not be enough to cover dividends.

DFDV's common stock traded near $4.41 on Monday, a market value of about $140 million—roughly half the value of its SOL, though it also carries debt. When a treasury company trades below its crypto stash, selling shares to buy tokens stops making sense, one reason the sector is under pressure.

CHAD holders will keep collecting $0.00516 per share for each business day through October 30, and the next macro test arrives Wednesday with the U.S. September inflation report.

title: Why Bitcoin Can Fall Before a Fed Rate Hike, Then Rally After It Happens
summary: Bitcoin fell on rate hike rumors, then rallied after the Fed acted. Learn why markets price the future and how crypto fits into the investment mix.
content:
Wall Street has an old saying: buy the rumor, sell the news. Bitcoin seems to be doing the opposite in 2026. It took a beating this September as traders bet on a Fed rate hike, then rallied once the Fed actually pulled the trigger. Sounds backward, but it makes more sense than it looks.

The answer lies in how markets price the future and how Bitcoin fits into the investment mix. Rate hikes reshape the competition for investor dollars, and crypto has a complicated relationship with risk. Let's break down the moving parts.

Every investor is shopping around. When rates rise, Treasury bonds, savings accounts and CDs start paying more, and a guaranteed yield suddenly looks a lot better than an asset that pays nothing. Bitcoin doesn't generate interest or dividends. Its only payoff is the price going up, which makes it a tougher sell when the alternatives get more generous.

Higher rates also tend to weigh on risk assets like stocks and crypto. Bitcoin was pitched by some as a hedge against market turmoil, but its track record looks more like a traditional risk asset. In a Federal Reserve speech on crypto and financial stability, then-Vice Chair Lael Brainard said crypto assets had shown a high correlation with riskier stocks and overall investor risk appetite.

In plain terms, when stocks get jittery over expensive money, Bitcoin usually gets jittery right along with them.

Markets hate uncertainty more than they hate bad news. When rumors started swirling this summer that the Fed might have to hike, risk assets sold off. Bitcoin, being as volatile as it is, took a particularly hard hit.

Then the Fed actually moved. On Sept. 16, it raised its target range by a quarter of a percentage point, its first increase in more than three years. Bitcoin didn't collapse. By the next morning, CoinDesk reported that it had climbed modestly above $76,000.

The explanation is simple. Much of the bad news was already priced in, and the hike wasn't worse than expected. Attention quickly shifted to what the Fed would do next. The Fed's September projections pointed to only limited additional increases, which eased fears of a string of aggressive hikes. Bitcoin responded with a relief rally.

The same logic shows up when you look at a different stretch of the year. In July, some market participants were bracing for a rate hike, then inflation came in cooler than expected. In reaction to this news on July 15, Bitcoin jumped about 3.6%, per CoinDesk .

The mechanics ran in reverse. When investors think rates are less likely to rise, safe income-producing assets lose some of their pull, and riskier assets like Bitcoin get breathing room.

Rate expectations are a major driver, but not the only one. Supply and demand, geopolitical events, ETF flows, regulation and crypto-specific news all shape the price. And often, what traders expect matters more than what actually happens.

Bitcoin's reaction to Fed policy is a useful reminder that prices move on expectations long before the official announcement. If you're watching the Fed to time your crypto moves, you're not alone, but you're competing with a lot of people who are doing the same thing. Before you bet on the next rate decision, make sure your position still makes sense if the Fed does the opposite of what you expect.

title: Solana Beat Bitcoin, Ethereum and XRP Over the Month and Lost to All Three This Week. One of Those Streaks Is About to End.
summary: Solana dominated its rivals over the past month but got crushed the same week its biggest upgrade went live. Two competing streaks cannot both survive October, and the clock is running out for one of them.
content:
Solana gained 9.9% over 30 days, beating Bitcoin's 8% gain, but reversed sharply with an 8.2% weekly drop, which was the worst performance among the four major cryptos.

Solana trades at $111, up 1.9% in the past 24 hours. While these figures overlap significantly, they reveal contrasting trends. Which trend is more reliable, and which may change first?

Many holders credit Solana's strong month to a recent network upgrade. On October 10, Solana reduced its block times to just 200 milliseconds, making it the fastest major blockchain. Block time refers to how quickly the network adds new entries to its ledger, the official record of all transactions. Faster block times let trades and payments settle more quickly for exchanges, payment apps, and trading bots on Solana.

While this upgrade is a major talking point for holders, price increases still require ongoing buyer demand; faster block times alone cannot create it. The upgrade's timing and the monthly gains overlap but do not necessarily indicate a direct cause-and-effect relationship.

Notably, Solana posted the largest drop among the four major cryptocurrencies during the week of its network upgrade. Holders who anticipated the upgrade still saw their investment decline relative to Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP.

Compared to Bitcoin, whose market has a deeper pool of buyers, Solana has less liquidity. When buyers pull back, Solana's price drops more sharply because fewer bids are available to support it. Conversely, when buyers return, Solana's price can rise faster for the same reason. This dynamic explains why Solana outperformed Bitcoin in a rising market but fell harder when the market turned.

For context, Solana is currently 62.0% below its all-time high and would need to multiply by 2.6 to reach that peak again. The latest month's gains and recent drops have only slightly changed the distance from its all-time high.

Currently, Solana's 30-day lead over Bitcoin seems most likely to end. The lead is narrow, and the recent poor performance now factors into the 30-day calculations, while earlier gains will soon drop off as the timeframe progresses. Furthermore, significant outflows on six of the seven trading days suggest the money supporting Solana's lead is exiting. The recent 1.9% bounce in 24 hours is too small to suggest a significant turnaround.

If Bitcoin maintains its stronger performance, as suggested by a 3.2% drop over the past week, Solana's lead could diminish. The critical observation period ends on October 31. If Solana's 30-day performance still surpasses Bitcoin's by then, and inflows return to Solana funds in the remaining days of October, we may need to rethink our view and treat the recent downturn as a temporary pause. title: Bitcoin Spooked? Crypto Fear and Greed Index Drops to Pre-Rally August Lows
summary: The Crypto Fear and Greed Index has dropped to 56 from an August peak of 82, as oil, bond yields, and ETF outflows hit Bitcoin in October.
content:
After a red hot summer lifted Bitcoin and the rest of crypto out of a brutal bear market, sentiment has now clearly shifted, bucking typically reliable seasonal trends.

Bitcoin is now trading just above $82,000, down close to 5% for the week, and the cryptocurrency market's Fear and Greed Index fell to 56 on Monday, a "neutral" reading, after reaching "extreme greed" in late August.

The Fear and Greed Index is a 0-to-100 gauge that measures investor appetite, where 0 is extreme fear and 100 extreme greed. The index peaked at 82 on Aug. 26, its high for the year, and read 68 a month ago.

Bitcoin peaked at $86,978 early last week and slid as low as $81,749.83 on Oct. 8, a drop of about 6%, before recovering to roughly $83,800 on Monday. That leaves the largest cryptocurrency about 34% below its all-time high of above $126,000, set on Oct. 6, 2025 back when extreme greed was the norm.

That slide marked a rough stretch that extended until August of this year. The August rally led to a 24.9% increase in the price of Bitcoin, enough for industry participants such as Fundstrat co-founder and Bitmine Chairman Tom Lee and Crypto Quant's Kim Yong Yu to announce the end of the bear market.

But the increased appetite for crypto bets has now cooled, at least for now, as the Fear and Greed Index indicates.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $484.9 million last week on Wednesday, their worst day since June, and another $244.1 million the following day. A $21.1 million inflow on Friday left the funds down a net $386.3 million for October while Ethereum funds extended their outflow streak to nine days, with $635 million out this month.

In terms of catalysts, macroeconomic headwinds have weighed on Bitcoin and the rest of crypto.

Brent crude topped $101 a barrel last week as ship attacks around the Strait of Hormuz piled up, and the 30-year Treasury yield hit 5.70%, its highest since 2002. Stocks, gold and Bitcoin sold off together that day, which points to a macro trade rather than a crypto problem. Brent is trading near $110 today, even after President Donald Trump said the U.S. would not engage in war at least until November.

Oil is an input cost for shipping, manufacturing, farming and travel, so a sustained jump in crude tends to filter into consumer prices. Higher inflation makes it harder for the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates and more likely to raise them, which is the path the central bank's latest minutes describe.

Bond investors respond by demanding higher yields, since inflation erodes the fixed payments Treasuries make. Because the Treasury yield is the benchmark "risk-free" return, a 30-year paying 5.70% pulls money away from riskier bets and raises borrowing costs across the economy. Bitcoin pays no yield and trades alongside stocks as a risk asset, so rising yields and rate-hike expectations tend to push it lower, as they did on Oct. 7.

The background likely explains why the Fear and Greed Index has dropped so much. Traders are more cautious, especially with high risk assets such as Bitcoin.

Traders on Myriad , a prediction market developed by Decrypt's parent company Dastan, give Bitcoin a 45% chance of touching $87,500 in October. That is down from 55% on Oct. 7. The odds of Bitcoin reaching $90,000 have slipped to 28% from 36%.

Myriad traders are also now pricing in 56% odds that Bitcoin drops to as low as $80,000, followed by 33% odds for a drop to $77,500 and 20% odds on $75,000.

title: XRP Is 3% of the Crypto Market. Ripple Has Spent Years Signing Bank Deals to Change That Number. Here Is What Moved It Instead.
summary: Ripple has spent years inking deals with banks and payment giants, yet XRP's slice of the crypto market keeps telling a different story. The forces actually shifting XRP's dominance have almost nothing to do with those partnerships.
content:
The November 2024 rally, SEC lawsuit resolution, and XRP ETF launches drove XRP's market share gains while Ripple's bank deals delivered nothing.

Banks can use Ripple's payment tech or its RLUSD stablecoin without holding XRP, so partnerships don't generate coin demand.

XRP is down 23% year-to-date despite partnership news, and only ETF inflows or a broad altcoin rally are likely to reverse that.

XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) currently holds a 3.14% share of the overall cryptocurrency market, a figure Ripple has worked hard to increase through partnerships with banks and payment companies. Valued at $1.40, XRP has a market capitalization of about $88.5 billion, compared to a total crypto market cap of roughly $2.81 trillion.

Over the past week, XRP has declined 7.7%, though it has gained 2.6% over the past month. It remains 61.6% below its all-time high. In October 2026, XRP's price fluctuated between $1.32 and $1.56.

Ripple promotes its partnerships by positioning XRP as a bridge asset for international money transfers, with everyday use driving its market position. However, the coin's market share has fluctuated over the years. So what drives these shifts, and what could change XRP's market share going forward?

Crypto dominance refers to a coin's market value divided by the total value of all cryptocurrencies. Market value, or market cap, is calculated by multiplying the coin's price by the number of coins in circulation. Thus, XRP's market share changes when its price fluctuates or when the overall crypto market shifts.

To provide context, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) commands 59.49% of the market, while Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) holds 11.06%. This leaves XRP at 3.14%, trailing well behind both.

Market trends show XRP's share dipped to around 1.5% in late 2022, then surged to nearly 4% in early 2025 before slipping again. While these figures are approximate, they illustrate a general trend.

Many investors mistakenly believe a rise in market share equals a rise in price, but the two don't necessarily go hand in hand. During market downturns, a coin can gain market share simply by declining less than other cryptocurrencies. For instance, if Bitcoin's price drops more steeply than XRP's, XRP's dominance may increase even as its holders face losses.

Three significant events have led to the most notable shifts in XRP's market share:

The Crypto Rally in November 2024: XRP closed October 2024 at $0.51 and then skyrocketed to $1.94 by the end of November. The overall market rose during this period, but XRP outperformed many coins, gaining market share as buyers became more willing to invest.

Resolution of the SEC Lawsuit in 2025: The Securities and Exchange Commission's conclusion of its lawsuit against Ripple lifted a significant overhang that had kept many cautious buyers at bay. While the direct impact is difficult to quantify, the conclusion likely encouraged new investment in XRP.

Introduction of Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) for XRP: These XRP ETFs, which trade on stock exchanges, provide a new pathway for investors to buy XRP through traditional brokerage accounts, bypassing the need for crypto exchange accounts.

Despite genuine growth and numerous announcements of Ripple's bank partnerships over the years, XRP's market share hasn't responded positively. This is because banks can utilize Ripple's payment technology or its stablecoin, pegged to the U.S. dollar, without needing to hold XRP. Consequently, these partnerships only boost XRP's market share if they drive demand for the coin itself.

However, the networks established through these partnerships could potentially support future demand that hasn't yet materialized. The lack of immediate impact through October 2026 doesn't rule out that possibility in the coming years.

Additionally, XRP's market share may not reflect XRP-specific demand alone; it could also be influenced by shifts in investor interest from Bitcoin to leading altcoins (any cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin) during market rallies and back again during sell-offs.

The next significant change in XRP's market share will likely come from increased buying activity, either through XRP funds or as part of a larger altcoin rally. Headlines about bank partnerships probably won't have much effect. For investors, these funds offer a crucial demand channel, since every dollar that flows into them must buy XRP. XRP's 23.4% year-to-date drop supports this view, occurring amid partnership announcements without notable market-share gains.

If XRP's market share increases from 3.14% back toward the 4% mark seen in early 2025 alongside a rising price, it would indicate a genuine return of buyers. Conversely, if the next major partnership is announced and market share remains stagnant at or below 3.14%, it would further illustrate the disconnect between these partnerships and XRP's market performance.

title: Weekly Trading Data Show Crypto Markets May Expect Prices to Fall
summary: Stablecoin supply fell $856 million and DEX spot volume dropped 19% last week, hinting at weaker crypto demand.
content:
About $856 million in stablecoins left circulation last week, according to Lookonchain's weekly data.

Trading on decentralized exchanges slowed at the same time, but one group of traders did the opposite.

Traders park cash in stablecoins before buying Bitcoin or other coins, so a shrinking supply means less money ready to spend.

Most of the outflow came from Ethereum and Solana. They shed $726 million and $619 million in Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC), respectively, Lookonchain data shows.

Tron moved the other way, adding $526 million.

Notably, the total weekly decline equals roughly 0.3% of all stablecoins in circulation, according to DefiLlama.

So, with the decline accounting for less than 0.5%, does the decline alone prove investors are exiting crypto?

Decentralized exchanges (DEXs) are apps where users swap coins straight from their own wallets, with no company in the middle. Spot trading there fell 19.34% on a weekly basis, to $47.84 billion. Uniswap volume alone dropped 25.8%.

Perpetual futures moved in the opposite direction. These contracts let traders bet on prices rising or falling, often with borrowed money. Their DEX volume rose 8.2% to $149.39 billion.

The volume data does not show which way those traders are betting.

Listed companies, in turn, cut their combined holdings by a net 89 BTC, worth about $7.37 million. Bitcoin miner CleanSpark sold 173 BTC, and Silvia, Inc. sold 165 BTC.

MicroStrategy still added 250 BTC, as Saylor's firm slows purchases. Separately, BitMine bought 12,532 ETH worth $31.75 million, even as the company nears its ETH cap.

Bitcoin traded at $82,859 as of writing, down almost 5% in the last week. It remains below the $85,000 threshold for days now on thin trading.

Still, not every gauge weakened. Fees collected by crypto apps rose 4.44% week on week, led by Tether's $122.06 million. Next week's stablecoin figures will show whether the cash that left returns.

title: Chainlink Is Up 15% This Month and Ethereum Is Flat. Both Are Still More Than Half Below Their Highs. Which One Has the Shorter Road Back?
summary: Chainlink and Ethereum are both sitting more than halfway below their peaks, but the gap between them goes far beyond price. One coin needs to quadruple just to break even with its history, while the other carries a structural advantage that could make all the difference.
content:
Ethereum needs to nearly double to reclaim its all-time high, while Chainlink must quadruple from 75% below its peak.

Ethereum ETFs, trading since July 2024, attracted more inflows than Bitcoin ETFs in 2026, giving ETH a far larger institutional investor base.

Chainlink's node operators receive LINK as payment and may sell immediately, limiting price gains even as network usage grows.

Chainlink (CRYPTO:LINK) rose 15.4% in the last 30 days, while Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) gained only 1.1%. Despite these movements, both cryptocurrencies are trading more than half below their all-time highs. This raises an intriguing question: which coin is actually closer to reclaiming its peak? In the Chainlink vs. Ethereum debate, one has the distance advantage, while the other benefits from recent momentum.

As of October 12, 2026, Chainlink is priced around $13, which is 74.8% below its all-time high of $53. In contrast, Ethereum is trading at about $2,551, or 48.4% below its peak of $4,946. Both coins fell over the past week, with Chainlink down 6.3% and Ethereum down 6.4%.

So, which coin has a shorter journey back to its all-time high?

A blockchain cannot see data outside its own records. For instance, a lending application on Ethereum cannot determine the dollar value of its collateral unless an external service provides that information. Chainlink serves as that vital service, functioning as an oracle network that supplies data like pricing directly to blockchains. Additionally, it facilitates the movement of tokens between different blockchains.

Applications that utilize Chainlink's services pay fees in LINK. As more apps depend on Chainlink for data and token transfers, the network generates higher revenue in its own token.

------

Meanwhile, Ethereum is the network where many of these applications operate. Demand comes from three primary sources: users pay transaction fees in ETH, investment funds buy ETH for their portfolios, and coin holders stake it. Staking involves locking up ETH to help secure the network in return for rewards.

This distinction influences how each coin recovers. Chainlink's revenue grows with usage, while Ethereum can attract demand from buyers who don't actively use the network, such as institutional investors.

To return to its all-time high, Ethereum needs to rise about 1.9 times, while Chainlink must rise about 4 times. Simply put, Ethereum has a shorter distance to cover.

However, when looking at recent momentum, Chainlink's 15.4% growth over 30 days far outpaces Ethereum's 1.1%. This aligns with the recent trend of traders shifting their focus toward altcoins. Yet the past week shows how quickly a rally can end, with both coins declining over the same period.

Chainlink does have an advantage in size. Smaller coins often require less new capital to achieve the same percentage increases as larger ones. Therefore, modest buying activity could propel LINK further than similar investments would affect ETH. Additionally, the rising trend of tokenizing traditional assets like bonds and fund shares needs the external price data and cross-chain transfer services that Chainlink provides.

Both cryptocurrencies now have spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that trade on traditional stock exchanges and hold the respective cryptocurrencies for investors. Grayscale debuted the first U.S. Chainlink ETF on December 2, 2025, followed by Bitwise on January 14. Nevertheless, Ethereum ETFs are more established and significantly larger, having traded since July 2024 and attracting more investment than Bitcoin ETFs in 2026.

The size of these funds dictates how much external capital can flow into the coins. Many retirement accounts, financial advisors, and institutions with strict custody guidelines cannot hold cryptocurrencies directly, opting instead to buy them through brokerage accounts. The larger Ethereum's funds grow, the more institutional money can be funneled into ETH.

Chainlink's revenue model does have a potential drawback. Fees paid in LINK do not guarantee lasting demand for the token, as the node operators who receive LINK as payment may sell it immediately. If selling pressure exceeds buying activity, then growth in network usage may not positively impact the token's price as much as anticipated.

In our view, Ethereum has the shorter road back to its high. It only needs to rise 1.9 times, compared to Chainlink's 4 times. Moreover, Ethereum's established funds have access to a much larger investor base. While Chainlink's recent 30-day growth is impressive, momentum can wane quickly. In contrast, recovery distance and fund demand shift more gradually.

For Chainlink holders, this means waiting for several conditions to align, including increased tokenization and apps that hold onto the LINK they purchase. Ethereum's path appears more straightforward. Its 1.1% growth over the past month needs to translate into a sustained upward trend, with increased network usage, staking, and demand from its funds pulling in the same direction.

With steady cash inflows into the Grayscale and Bitwise Chainlink funds, the dynamics could shift and change our outlook. Until then, Ethereum seems poised to reclaim its all-time high first in this Chainlink vs. Ethereum comparison.

After the latest purchases, $354.8 million remains under Strategy's digital credit securities repurchase program. The board doubled that program to $2 billion in September. A separate $1.0 billion authorization for MSTR shares is untouched.

title: Strategy buys $21 million worth of Bitcoin as corporate crypto buying shows signs of revival
summary: Bitcoin’s rebound has turned some corporate sellers back into buyers after months of market turmoil.
content:
Bitcoin buying is back. Corporate crypto heavyweight Strategy announced Monday that it bought over $21 million worth of Bitcoin last week, bringing its total holdings to roughly $70 billion. The company, led by flamboyant billionaire Michael Saylor , funded the purchase by selling more than 125,000 shares of its common stock and using $500,000 in cash. It also spent roughly $192 million to repurchase nearly 2 million shares of STRC, a type of preferred stock that makes regular payments to investors.

The latest purchase extends Strategy's return to Bitcoin buying, marking its fifth purchase since August.

Bitcoin broke out of a prolonged trading lull in mid-August, climbing to around $77,000 for the first time since May. It has largely held above that level since and was trading at $82,600 Monday morning. The rebound followed a steep downturn that pushed Bitcoin from a high of $126,000 last October to a low of $58,000 in June. Amid the slump, Strategy—which holds roughly 4% of Bitcoin's circulating supply—sold portions of its stockpile on four occasions. As Bitcoin's price rebounded, Strategy stopped selling and returned to stockpiling.

Strategy isn't the only big player wading back into Bitcoin. Other companies have recently added crypto to their balance sheets, breathing life back into corporate crypto buying .

Earlier this month, Strive, the asset manager cofounded by billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, announced a $169 million purchase of 2,000 Bitcoin, bringing its stockpile to roughly $2.4 billion. Robinhood, the crypto trading platform led by CEO Vlad Tenev, also joined the ranks of corporate Bitcoin buyers and recently disclosed a $25 million investment for its own balance sheet. Metaplanet, the Japanese investment firm and world's second-largest publicly traded Bitcoin treasury company, announced this month that it sold 10,000 Bitcoin and bought 11,000 in the third quarter to demonstrate to credit markets that it could convert its holdings into cash when needed.

But companies aren't just stockpiling Bitcoin. Bitmine, a Bitcoin miner turned into an Ethereum treasury company, announced this month that it had added roughly $41 million worth of the cryptocurrency to its treasury. The purchase brought its holdings to about 6 million tokens—nearly 5% of Ether's total supply.

The renewed buying comes as Bitcoin's recovery fuels hopes of further gains. The cryptocurrency has held up despite recent interest rate hikes in the United States and renewed tensions in the Middle East.

title: Would a Bitcoin Standard Slow Economic Growth? What Willy Woo Argues
summary: An analyst says Bitcoin's fixed supply makes borrowing riskier and slows growth, answering a challenge from The Bitcoin Standard author.
content:
Bitcoin (BTC) analyst Willy Woo has offered an answer to a challenge that economist Saifedean Ammous first posed in 2019. Woo argues that Bitcoin's fixed supply makes borrowing riskier, which could slow economic growth.

Ammous, author of the book The Bitcoin Standard, reposted his original call on X. He says he is still waiting for an economist to explain clearly why a hard-capped money would fail. His 2019 post asked for an argument beyond "snarky eyerolls." However, the most detailed reply so far came from a crypto analyst, not an academic.

Woo ties the problem with Bitcoin's fixed supply directly to debt. When a currency keeps rising in value, borrowers must repay loans in money that grows more expensive. As a result, the risk of default climbs, and lenders pull back.

He points to the current wave of global borrowing for AI infrastructure as an example of debt-fueled growth. Some investors already warn that the AI data center boom could end in a crash.

History offers a parallel. Under the gold standard, he notes, the ratio of paper money to gold backing rose to ease lending risk. That shift kept credit flowing on top of a scarce reserve asset.

Woo does not frame the cost of Bitcoin's fixed supply as purely negative. A Bitcoin standard that uses satoshis, the smallest BTC unit, would likely deliver much slower growth. Yet it would also produce far fewer bubbles, he says.

One user countered that savings build capital from the bottom up. Woo disagreed, saying growth relies on tech, energy, and raw materials. Those need mega-scale infrastructure and large pools of capital.

Woo has previously argued that Bitcoin may follow a 6-8 year debt cycle.

The exchange revives an old divide. Bitcoin advocates often cite the dollar's lost purchasing power as the case for hard money. Critics, in contrast, see Bitcoin's fixed supply as a brake on credit.

Woo's answer suggests both camps describe the same mechanism from opposite ends. The real question is whether a sats-based economy would trade faster growth for fewer bubbles.

title: French MPs push exit tax on crypto above €800,000 and fines for undeclared wallets
summary: French MPs want wealthy crypto investors who leave the country to pay tax on their paper gains, under an amendment backed in committee last week alongside fines of up to €10,000 for undeclared self-custody wallets, though every measure must be voted on again.View on euronews
content:
Moving abroad from France could soon cost the richest holders of digital assets more, as lawmakers seek to bring Bitcoin and other crypto into a levy already paid by relocating equity investors.

On Thursday, the National Assembly's finance committee, the cross-party panel that vets budget bills before the full lower house debates them, voted to extend France's exit tax to crypto-assets from 1 January 2027.

The current levy taxes unrealised gains when people who have lived in France for at least six of the past ten years move abroad with shares and other securities cumulatively worth more than €800,000.

The amendment would apply the same threshold to a household's crypto, including tokens on foreign platforms or in self-custody wallets that owners control directly.

As with shares, payment would be deferred for moves within the EU and to some other countries, and the tax is cancelled if the assets are kept for two to five years.

The amendment does not set a rate or mention social charges, which make up 18.6 points of the 31.4% levied on departing shareholders' gains, leaving unclear what crypto holders would pay.

Its sponsors, Communist MP Nicolas Sansu and 16 left-wing colleagues, argue that crypto escapes a levy applied to securities of equal value, inviting tax avoidance.

The committee also backed a plan by centrist MP Charles de Courson to make taxpayers declare self-custody wallets worth a combined €100,000 or more at year-end, or face fines of up to €10,000. Currently, only crypto accounts abroad must be reported.

Citing a parliamentary inquiry that flagged crypto as a fraud risk, its backers say French investors made an estimated €3.5 billion in crypto gains in 2021 but declared only €400 million in holdings.

France's Court of Audit has said that figure was in fact declared gains.

Related

ECB launches 'Pontes' to settle tokenised assets in central bank money

ECB calls for tougher EU crypto rules and wider ban on stablecoin interest

Crypto advocates warn such a data register could leak and endanger holders, amid a wave of crypto-linked kidnappings in France.

Police counted more than 40 crypto-linked kidnappings in France between January and mid-April, after about 30 in all of 2025.

In one of the best-known cases, kidnappers seized David Balland, co-founder of French crypto wallet maker Ledger, and his partner in January 2025, cutting off one of his fingers to press a crypto ransom demand before police freed them.

A second Sansu amendment, which also sets no rate, would make swapping crypto for stablecoins, tokens pegged to a currency such as the US dollar, taxable from 2027 under the existing 31.4% flat tax on crypto gains.

Tax is currently only due on cashing out or spending crypto.

MPs also voted to let investors offset crypto losses against gains for ten years and to raise a planned fine for ignoring tax authority requests for documents from €10,000 to €50,000 per request. The government's bill applies it to financial institutions, crypto firms and online platforms.

The committee rejected a broader wealth tax including crypto and a bid by centre-right MP Paul Midy to make up to €1,000 a year of crypto payments tax-free.

On Friday, the committee voted down the revenue part of the government's 2027 budget bill, which covers taxes, by 31 votes to 3.

France's constitution requires the full Assembly to debate the government's original budget, with committee changes normally put to MPs as amendments.

With the revenue part rejected, none carry over, so the crypto amendments must be re-tabled from Tuesday.

Related

France's public debt soars to a record 119% of GDP

France's borrowing rate keeps rising, hitting its highest level since 2002

MPs vote again on the revenue part on 20 October and the whole bill on 17 November, before the Senate takes over. Last year, they threw out the revenue part by 404 votes to 1, wiping out their changes.

The French Parliament has until 10 December to pass the budget, after which the government can enact it by ordinance.

With France's 10-year borrowing costs briefly topping 5% this month for the first time since 2002 and parties eyeing next spring's presidential election, the minority government faces an uphill battle to pass the budget.

title: Bitcoin Has Closed Four Straight Weeks Above Its 50-Week Average. The Last Time It Did That It Tripled Within a Year.
summary: A rare pattern in Bitcoin's price history has only appeared twice before, and each time it triggered a dramatic move in completely opposite directions. Which outcome the current streak mirrors could define the next year for Bitcoin holders.
content:
Bitcoin has closed above its 50-week average ($76,618) for four straight weeks, trading at $83,369 as of October 12, 2026.

The last two times this signal triggered, Bitcoin surged 217% in 2023 but crashed 50% after an initial 170% gain in 2019.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) has closed above its 50-week average for four straight weeks. As of October 12, 2026, Bitcoin is trading at $83,369, while its 50-week average sits at $76,618. If it closes below this average, it would end this current streak.

This indicator has appeared twice in the last decade, each time producing very different outcomes. In January 2023, Bitcoin climbed above the average near $23,000 and rose 217% to a high of around $73,000 by March 2024. Conversely, in April 2019, it rebounded to near $5,000 and initially surged 170% to about $13,800 by June, but then fell about 50% to about $6,500 by December of that same year.

So what does a fourth consecutive weekly close above the average suggest about what might happen next for Bitcoin holders?

The 50-week average is calculated by averaging Bitcoin's closing prices for the past 50 weeks. It helps smooth out price fluctuations, giving a clearer picture of longer-term trends. When Bitcoin stays above this average, it indicates that buyers are dominating the market. If it trades below, it suggests sellers are in control.

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

The 'weekly close' refers to the last price at the end of each trading week. Traders typically regard this price as more significant than daily closes because it reduces market noise. Since Bitcoin is traded around the clock, a sudden price spike on a single day can briefly push the price above or below the average before reverting back. A weekly close counts only if Bitcoin is above the line when the week ends.

When Bitcoin achieves four consecutive weekly closes above this average, it sets a higher standard. A single close might be a temporary bounce, but four consecutive ones show buyers have consistently held the price up.

The 2023 signal is often touted as a success story. When Bitcoin reclaimed its 50-week average near $23,000 in January 2023, it skyrocketed 217% to roughly $73,000 by March 2024. Those who interpreted this signal as the start of a new uptrend were vindicated.

In contrast, the 2019 signal began similarly. After regaining the average near $5,000 in April 2019, it rose to about $13,800 by June—a significant increase. However, this rally was short-lived: Bitcoin fell about 50% to about $6,500 by December, leaving those who held through the year disappointed.

Analysts attribute these differences to factors like liquidity, the amount of money flowing into riskier investments, and the timing of halving events, when the rate of new Bitcoin production is reduced. However, with only two instances to reference, these explanations remain speculative.

Bitcoin is currently about 33.9% below its record high of $126,080. It has risen 8.0% over the past 30 days but fallen 3.2% in the last week. This mix of trends could indicate a scenario similar to either of the previous signals.

The 50-week average is always changing. Each week, the oldest closing price drops out of the calculation while the most recent price is included, slightly altering the average Bitcoin needs to maintain.

This four-week streak strongly suggests Bitcoin's trend may be shifting upward. However, it doesn't necessarily indicate how far the price will rise or how long this trend will last. Both past signals preceded significant gains, but one of those gains was largely lost by the year's end.

For now, holders should pay close attention. A weekly close below the average, currently around $76,618, would end the streak and suggest a shift back towards a downtrend. Until then, either a repeat of the 2023 rally or a downturn like 2019 remains possible.

title: MicroStrategy's Bitcoin Buys Drop 84% in 2 Weeks. Why Is Saylor Slowing Down?

content:
Strategy, the Nasdaq-listed company that holds more Bitcoin (BTC) than any other public firm, bought just 250 coins last week. Its stack now stands at 848,250 BTC.

Two weeks ago, the company formerly known as MicroStrategy added 1,665 BTC. Last week it bought 334, making this its second smaller purchase in a row.

The latest 250 BTC cost about $21.5 million, at an average of $86,194 per coin, according to the filing. For scale, Strategy bought 55,500 BTC in a single week in November 2024.

The slowdown does not reflect an empty bank account. MicroStrategy held about $4.9 billion in its dollar reserve, a cash pile set aside for dividends, according to its October 5 filing.

Instead, more of its money has gone into buying back its own shares. In the week to October 4, it spent $176.3 million repurchasing Stretch (STRC), a preferred stock that pays investors a monthly dividend.

That was roughly six times its Bitcoin spend, as BeInCrypto reported in its coverage of last week's buyback-heavy filing. A week earlier, STRC buybacks of $151.7 million also topped the $142.7 million spent on Bitcoin.

Bitcoin trades near $83,283, up 0.19% in 24 hours, according to BeInCrypto's Bitcoin price page.

At that price, Strategy's coins are worth about $70.61 billion. Its average cost is $75,441 per coin. Gold advocate Peter Schiff argued that Strategy has lost its buying power because the STRC share sales that once funded its purchases have dried up.

Saylor has not slowed his signaling, however. He teased this purchase on Sunday with his usual chart of orange dots, one for each buy.

Strategy still has about $18.8 billion of common stock it is authorized to sell, according to its September 28 filing. Its next filings will show how much of that money goes to Bitcoin and how much to buybacks.

The 10-year Treasury yield stands at 5.24% and the 30-year yield at 5.60%, according to CNBC, having hit 52-week highs of 5.37% and 5.73% last week. Yields reached their highest levels in more than two decades, CoinShares head of research James Butterfill wrote on Thursday.

Butterfill argued that if those yields increasingly reflect concerns about U.S. public finances rather than stronger growth, Bitcoin begins to look "less like a conventional risk asset and more like an alternative to government-issued money."

"The recent easing of Middle East tensions has provided some breathing room, but the sustainability of the rebound will depend on whether the improvement in sentiment translates into a more meaningful retreat in bond yields and the dollar," Hathorn said. title: Wall Street’s Blockchain Boom Could Leave Bitcoin and Ethereum Behind — Here Are 5 Cryptos to Watch
summary: Citrini Research argues that Wall Street's blockchain expansion could create better investment opportunities than Bitcoin and Ethereum alone. CCN examines five cryptocurrencies that could benefit ...
content:
Key Takeaways

Citrini Research argues that Wall Street's blockchain expansion could create better investment opportunities than Bitcoin and Ethereum alone.

CCN examines five cryptocurrencies that could benefit from the Wall Street boom.

The firm warns that greater institutional adoption of blockchain does not necessarily translate into higher token prices.

Wall Street's move onto blockchain could create a new generation of crypto winners, but Bitcoin and Ethereum may not capture the biggest gains.

That's the investment thesis emerging from an Oct. 8 report by Citrini Research, which argues that the convergence of artificial intelligence and tokenized financial assets could transform global markets.

In its 79-page report, Breaking the Wall, the firm suggests the biggest opportunities may lie with platforms that profit from trading and other financial activity as traditional assets move on-chain.

For much of its existence, crypto has struggled to establish a compelling use case beyond speculation, according to Citrini.

The firm argues that decentralized finance has largely operated separately from traditional markets, limiting its ability to serve investors seeking exposure to stocks and other established assets.

However, that separation is now beginning to change.

In its Oct. 8 report, Citrini points to the growing tokenization of traditional financial assets and the emergence of AI as two developments that could accelerate blockchain adoption.

"Blockchains have finally found their raison d'être," the firm wrote.

Tokenization allows conventional financial assets to be represented digitally on blockchain networks, potentially enabling them to move between applications.

That could create opportunities for decentralized exchanges and other services built around those assets.

However, Citrini's central question is not simply whether blockchain adoption will accelerate, but who stands to profit from it.

Citrini argues that the shift toward blockchain-based financial markets is no longer purely theoretical.

Its report highlights the growing availability of tokenized financial instruments, including equities, government securities and commodities.

Citrini highlighted the introduction of Robinhood's Stock Tokens as a development that is helping expand tokenized equities beyond individual trading platforms.

"This has snowballed to more chains," Citrini wrote.

That could allow financial assets to interact with trading applications rather than remain confined to a single provider.

For example, a supported tokenized security could potentially be transferred between compatible platforms.

Citrini also pointed to Hyperliquid's role during the March escalation of the Iran conflict, when traders used blockchain derivatives to gain exposure to oil price movements outside conventional market hours.

The firm described the episode as an early indication of blockchain's growing relevance to financial markets.

"Since then, RWA adoption has really shifted into higher gear," the report stated.

However, blockchain trading volumes do not necessarily represent the same type of activity as conventional securities markets.

Citrini Research argues that Wall Street's blockchain expansion could create major investment opportunities without necessarily sending Bitcoin and Ethereum to new highs.

"We can't assume that majors, primarily BTC and ETH, will make new ATHs on this," Citrini wrote, according to CoinDesk.

"Even if they do, there are better expressions."

Bitcoin's investment appeal remains closely tied to its role as a store of value and scarcity, while Ethereum provides infrastructure for smart contracts.

However, Citrini argues that the biggest opportunities may lie with platforms that generate revenue as traditional financial assets move onto blockchain networks.

"The relevant question for any investor isn't simply whether more assets become tokenized. It's where the economics accrue," the firm wrote.

For example, decentralized lending platforms could earn fees from loans backed by tokenized securities.

Those financial benefits would not necessarily flow directly to BTC or ETH holders.

Citrini's research examines a broader range of crypto projects positioned to benefit from tokenization.

CCN has selected five cryptocurrencies from the projects discussed in coverage of Citrini's research, examining how each could benefit from Wall Street's blockchain expansion.

Chainlink could play an important role in connecting traditional financial institutions with blockchain networks.

Its infrastructure allows decentralized applications to access external information, including financial market data.

That capability could become increasingly valuable if tokenized stocks and other securities begin moving between blockchain-based financial platforms.

However, growing demand for Chainlink's services does not necessarily guarantee equivalent growth in LINK's market value.

The investment case depends partly on how increased network usage translates into demand for the token.

Ondo Finance represents one of the more direct connections between crypto and traditional financial markets.

The company has developed products designed to provide blockchain-based exposure to conventional financial instruments, including US government securities.

Its broader expansion into tokenized financial products places it within the market Citrini believes could grow substantially.

If investors increasingly seek access to traditional assets through blockchain networks, platforms such as Ondo could attract additional activity.

However, the success of Ondo's financial products does not automatically translate into financial returns for ONDO holders.

Aave could benefit from another potential consequence of tokenization: the ability to borrow against financial assets without having to sell them.

The decentralized lending protocol already allows users to deposit supported cryptocurrencies and borrow other assets against their holdings.

As tokenization expands, similar arrangements could potentially support a wider range of financial instruments.

For example, an investor holding eligible tokenized securities might eventually be able to use those assets as collateral within decentralized lending markets.

However, this would depend on the assets being supported by the relevant lending platform and meeting its risk requirements.

Regulatory restrictions, liquidity concerns, and collateral valuation risks could also limit adoption.

Uniswap could become another beneficiary if traditional financial instruments increasingly trade through decentralized exchanges.

The protocol allows users to exchange supported digital assets through liquidity pools rather than conventional order books.

A wider selection of tokenized securities could potentially increase demand for blockchain-based trading infrastructure.

However, the opportunity comes with substantial regulatory and commercial uncertainty.

Not all tokenized securities can legally be traded on permissionless exchanges , and financial institutions may prefer regulated trading venues.

There is also no guarantee that additional trading volume would directly increase UNI's value.

Maple Finance focuses on blockchain-based lending and financial products, making it another potential beneficiary of institutional adoption.

Unlike platforms primarily associated with retail crypto trading, Maple has developed services aimed at borrowers and investors seeking structured lending opportunities.

The expansion of tokenized financial assets could create additional opportunities for lending platforms to manage credit and collateral.

But lending growth introduces risks beyond crypto price volatility.

Borrower defaults and collateral losses could undermine returns even if institutional demand increases.

The disconnect between institutional adoption and crypto prices has become a recurring frustration among XRP holders.

Ripple has expanded its presence in traditional finance through acquisitions and financial services, but some investors have questioned how much of that success actually benefits XRP.

The concern has become particularly relevant as Ripple pushes deeper into Wall Street through its prime brokerage and institutional financing operations.

While these developments could strengthen Ripple's position in traditional finance, not all its services require customers to buy or use XRP.

That distinction illustrates a broader risk underlying Citrini's investment thesis.

A blockchain platform could attract substantial institutional activity without generating equivalent returns for holders.

Similar questions apply to the five alternative cryptocurrencies selected by CCN.

Decentralized exchanges could generate substantial trading fees without necessarily distributing those earnings to token holders.

Citrini's research suggests the next phase of blockchain adoption could look very different from previous crypto market cycles, with traditional financial assets and AI potentially driving demand .

"The worlds of traditional finance and crypto are merging," the firm wrote.

It argues that blockchain networks could increasingly support financial products used by mainstream institutions, while AI agents create demand for infrastructure that operates continuously.

"AI agents move programmatically, 24/7, across applications," the report stated.

However, the investment opportunity remains uncertain.

For investors considering smaller cryptocurrencies, the challenge is determining whether the platforms benefiting from tokenization will deliver meaningful economic value to their token holders.

Citrini's research suggests Wall Street's blockchain expansion could create a new generation of crypto winners.

But as Ripple's expansion into Wall Street demonstrates, winning institutional business does not necessarily mean winning over cryptocurrency investors.
